detect_tables_phase.system: You are a data engineer tasked to design an integrated schema that will be used to represent all data from a set of source tables.
detect_tables_phase.human:
You are at step 1. of the schema integration process. You are given a source table and your task is to identify the entity types present in the table and split the table if needed based on the types found.

[DEMONSTRATION]


<sourcetable>

[TABLE_INPUT]

</sourcetable>

<instruction>
 Your instructions are the following:
1. Identify the entity types described by the table.
2. Choose one main entity type that the table primarily describes.
3. Identify any other entity types that relate to the main entity.
4. For the main entity and each related entity, list the attributes (columns) that belong to it.
5. Split the table into multiple tables ONLY if there is low overlap between attribute groups.
6. This is not database normalization.
7. Do not split out an entity if it only has a single attribute related to it.
Return the schemata of all resulting output tables in the following JSON format {"<table_name>": {"attributes": ["<attribute1>", "<attribute2>", "..."]}}
Be brief in the naming of the output table and use general terms without parenthesis.
Use the original attribute names of the source table in the output tables.
Make sure that you do not generate tables with less than three attributes.
</instruction>Reply with the correct JSON format: The JSON must follow this exact schema: {"<table_name>": {"attributes": ["<attribute1>", "<attribute2>", "..."]}} Example: {"employee": {"attributes": ["employee_id", "employee_name", "employee_age"]}, "department": {"attributes": ["department_id", "department_name"]}}.

grouping_phase.system: You are a data engineer tasked to design an integrated schema that will be used to represent all data from a set of source tables.
grouping_phase.human:
You are at step 2 of the schema integration process and are given the set of tables that results from step 1. Your task is to group (cluster) the tables that describe the same entity type, so that all tables that describe the same or semantically similar entity types are put into the same group. Name each group according to the entity type of the grouped tables. If a hierarchy can be observed between the found groups, combine the tables that are connected through this hierarchy and name the overall group after the highest entity type in the hierarchy.

[DEMONSTRATION]


<set of tables to be grouped>
[TABLES]</set of tables to be grouped>

<instruction>Please group (cluster) the set of tables tables by entity type, so that all tables that describe the same or similar entity types are put into the same group. Return the names of the groups together with the names of the tables in each group strictly using the following JSON format {group_name: [names of tables in the group]} with no additional commentary.
Be brief in the naming of the groups and use general terms without parenthesis.
Make sure that each table is part of exactly one group.
The column headers overlap between the tables can also be used as a signal to help with the grouping.
Tables can't belong to multiple tables!
</instruction>

grouping_phase_with_correspondences.system: You are a data engineer tasked to design an integrated schema that will be used to represent all data from a set of source tables.
grouping_phase_with_correspondences.human:
You are at step 2 of the schema integration process and are given the set of tables that results from step 1 and the matching columns (correspondences) between the different tables. Your task is to group (cluster) the tables that describe the same entity type, so that all tables that describe the same or semantically similar entity types are put into the same group. If there are correspondences between tables and the context of the tables is the same, this means that the tables should most likely be grouped together. Name each group according to the entity type of the grouped tables. If a hierarchy can be observed between the found groups, combine the tables that are connected through this hierarchy and name the overall group after the highest entity type in the hierarchy.

[DEMONSTRATION]


<set of tables to be grouped>
[TABLES]</set of tables to be grouped><correspondences>

[CORRESPONDENCES]

</correspondences>

<instruction>Please group (cluster) the set of tables tables by entity type, so that all tables that describe the same or similar entity types are put into the same group. Return the names of the groups together with the names of the tables in each group strictly using the following JSON format {"group_name": [names of tables in the group]} with no additional commentary.
Be brief in the naming of the groups and use general terms without parenthesis.
Make sure that each table is part of exactly one group.
The overlaps of the attributes between the groups should be a signal for further merging.
</instruction>

schema_matching_phase.system: You are a data engineer tasked to design an integrated schema that will be used to represent all data from a set of source tables.
schema_matching_phase.human:
You are at a pre-step to step 3 of the schema integration process and your task is to perform schema matching i.e. find matching columns between the given source and target tables. Please find correspondences between the source and target columns of the input tables. Correspondences between columns mean that the column match semantically. For the columns to semantically match, they should also refer to the same semantic type. Do not match same attributes that refer to different entity types. Not all columns can have correspondences.

[DEMONSTRATION]


<input tables>
[TABLES]
</input tables>

<instruction>Please find the correspondences between the source and target tables and return them using the following JSON format {target_table_name: {source_table_column_name: matching_target_table_column_name}} with no additional commentary.
Do not return redundant correspondences e.g. if column x matches column y, return column x: column y and do not add column y: column x.
Return correspondences of the source table to the other target tables not the other way around!
</instruction> Reply only with the correct JSON format and no other comments!

schema_integration_phase.system: You are a data engineer tasked to design an integrated schema that will be used to represent all data from a set of source tables.
schema_integration_phase.human:
You are at step 3 of the schema integration process and are given a set of tables all describing the same entity type. First, identify the matching columns between the tables. Two columns match if they describe the same semantic concept. Afterwards, using these found matches, merge (integrate) the attributes and avoid adding to the final schema redundant attributes i.e. don't include two attributes of the same matching group in the final schema.

[DEMONSTRATION]


<set of tables to be integrated>

[TABLES]

</set of tables to be integrated>
<instruction>

Please merge (integrate) the schemata of all tables (i.e. merge the matching attributes) into a single integrated schema, that can be used to represent the data of all tables without losing any data. Return the schema of the integrated table and the mappings of the old attributes to the new ones strictly as JSON in the format {"<integrated_schema>": [list of integrated attributes], "<mappings_of_old_attributes>": {"<table_name>": {"<old_attribute>": "<integrated_attribute>"}}} with no additional commentary. Make sure that each attribute appears only once in the integrated schema.
Do not add the table names in the column name mappings.
</instruction> Return the correct JSON format.

schema_integration_phase_with_correspond.system: You are a data engineer tasked to design an integrated schema that will be used to represent all data from a set of source tables.
schema_integration_phase_with_correspond.human:
You are at step 3 of the schema integration process and are given a set of tables all describing the same entity type and their attributes are grouped based on correspondences found between the tables. Your task is to assign to each attribute grouping a representative attribute from the group.

[DEMONSTRATION]


<grouped tables>

[TABLES]

</grouped tables>
<groups_of_matching_attributes>[ATTRIBUTE_GROUPS]</groups_of_matching_attributes>

<instruction>

Please choose for each matching group of attributes a representative attribute among them and reply using the following JSON format: {"<group_name(replace with the group indentifier of an attribute group)>": "<representative_attribute(replace with the chosen attribute)>"} 
Do not mix the groupings!
Prefer choosing the attribute that can include all other attributes in the groups e.g. between year and date, date includes year so date should be chosen.</instruction> Reply only with the JSON format!

final_integration_phase.system: You are a data engineer tasked to design an integrated schema that will be used to represent all data from a set of source tables.
final_integration_phase.human:
You are at the end of the schema integration process. You are given a set of integrated schemas from step 3.
Examine the table schemata and the given relationships that exist between the schemata. This phase has two tasks: create identifiers for the tables IF needed (e.g. when more than one table schema is given) and remove redundant attributes, such as the same attribute appearing in the different tables. Remove redundant tables as well, e.g. if two tables can be merged together. When introducing identifiers, if there is a relationship between two table schemas (or more) use the identifiers as foreign keys and replace the old attributes.

<integrated schemata>

[SCHEMATA]

</integrated schemata>

<relationships>

[RELATIONSHIPS]

</relationships>
<instructions>
Do NOT add any new table schemata!
Add identifiers ONLY if needed (as foreign keys). If there are already existing identifiers do not add new ones.
Remove redundant attributes e.g. if the same attribute shows in two different table schemas and it is not used as a foreign key, decide on which table it should be left in.
When choosing foreign keys, base your decision on the previously recorded relationships between the table schemata given to you.
Return the final schemata of all tables strictly as JSON in the format {table_name: {attributes: [list of attributes], foreign_keys: {attribute_name: {other_table_name: other_attribute_name}}}}.
</instructions>

final_integration_phase_with_tables.system: You are a data engineer tasked to design an integrated schema that will be used to represent all data from a set of source tables.
final_integration_phase_with_tables.human:
You are at the end of the schema integration process. You are given a set of integrated schemas and a preview of the integrated tables following the integrated schemas from step 3.
Examine the table schemata and the given relationships that exist between the schemata. This phase has two tasks: create identifiers for the tables and remove redundant attributes. When introducing identifiers, if there is a relationship between two table schemas (or more) use the identifiers as foreign keys and replace the old attributes.

<integrated tables>

[TABLE_INPUT]

</integrated tables>

<integrated schemata>

[SCHEMATA]

</integrated schemata>

<relationships>

[RELATIONSHIPS]

</relationships>
<instructions>
Do NOT add any new table schemata!
Add identifiers for each table schema that can be used as foreign keys. If there are already existing identifiers do not add new ones. If there is only one table schema there is no need to add non-existing identifiers.
Remove redundant attributes e.g. if the same attribute shows in two different table schemas and it is not used as a foreign key, decide on which table it should be left in.
When choosing foreign keys, base your decision on the previously recorded relationships between the table schemata given to you.
Do not change the naming of the entities!
Return the final schemata of all tables strictly as JSON in the format {"table_name": {"attributes": [list of attributes], "foreign_keys": {"attribute_name": {"other_table_name": "other_attribute_name"}}}}.
</instructions> Reply only with the correct JSON and no other comments!

To determine the schema integration, I will analyze the attributes in the source table to identify distinct entity types.

1.  **Analyze Attributes and Entity Types:**
    *   **Event-related attributes:** `allDates`, `endDate`, `name` (Event Title), `description`, `price`, `image`, `website`, `moreInfoLink`. These clearly describe an event or activity.
    *   **Venue-related attributes:** `venueName`, `address`, `city`, `state`, `zipcode`, `latitude`, `longitude`. These describe the physical location where the event takes place.
    *   **Contact-related attributes:** `phone`, `email`. These are contact details. In many contexts, contact details belong to the entity being described (either the event organizer or the venue). Looking at the data:
        *   Row 2: Phone is present, Venue is "HaLo".
        *   Row 3: Phone and Email are present, Venue is "The Whiting".
        *   Row 1, 4, 5: Phone/Email are often missing or `nan`.
        *   It is reasonable to associate contact info (`phone`, `email`) with the **Venue** or the **Event** depending on context. However, since `venueName` is explicitly listed and often distinct from the event `name`, and contacts are frequently associated with the location (venue) in such datasets, let's evaluate the overlap.

2.  **Determine Main Entity:**
    The table primarily lists events (indicated by `name`, `description`, `dates`, `price`). The venue information is secondary but substantial.

3.  **Group Attributes by Entity:**
    *   **Event Entity:** `name`, `description`, `allDates`, `endDate`, `price`, `image`, `website`, `moreInfoLink`.
    *   **Venue Entity:** `venueName`, `address`, `city`, `state`, `zipcode`, `latitude`, `longitude`.
    *   **Contact Entity?** `phone`, `email`.

4.  **Evaluate Splitting Criteria:**
    *   **Overlap:** The attributes for Event and Venue are distinct. There is very low overlap between the set of event-specific columns and venue-specific columns.
    *   **Constraint Check:**
        *   **Event Table:** Attributes: `name`, `description`, `allDates`, `endDate`, `price`, `image`, `website`, `moreInfoLink`. Count: 8. (Valid, >= 3).
        *   **Venue Table:** Attributes: `venueName`, `address`, `city`, `state`, `zipcode`, `latitude`, `longitude`. Count: 7. (Valid, >= 3).
        *   **What about `phone` and `email`?**
            *   If we add `phone` and `email` to the **Venue** table: Venue attributes become `venueName`, `address`, `city`, `state`, `zipcode`, `latitude`, `longitude`, `phone`, `email`. Count: 9. This makes sense as venues have phone numbers and emails.
            *   If we add `phone` and `email` to the **Event** table: Event attributes become `name`, `description`, `allDates`, `endDate`, `price`, `image`, `website`, `moreInfoLink`, `phone`, `email`. Count: 10.
            *   Looking at the data:
                *   Row 2: Venue "HaLo" has a phone.
                *   Row 3: Venue "The Whiting" has a phone and email.
                *   Row 1: Venue is `nan`, Phone is `nan`.
                *   Row 4: Venue "Margaret Jenkins Dance Lab", Phone `nan`.
                *   Row 5: Venue "Browsers Coffee Shop", Phone `nan`.
            *   It is most logical to associate `phone` and `email` with the **Venue** because they appear when a specific venue name is present (Rows 2 and 3). Rows 1, 4, and 5 have venue names but no phone/email, or no venue name and no phone/email. This suggests the contact info belongs to the venue entity.

5.  **Final Grouping:**
    *   **Table 1: `event`**
        *   Attributes: `name`, `description`, `allDates`, `endDate`, `price`, `image`, `website`, `moreInfoLink`
    *   **Table 2: `venue`**
        *   Attributes: `venueName`, `address`, `city`, `state`, `zipcode`, `latitude`, `longitude`, `phone`, `email`

6.  **Verify Constraints:**
    *   `event` has 8 attributes. (>= 3)
    *   `venue` has 9 attributes. (>= 3)
    *   Split is justified due to low overlap between event details and venue/contact details.

Your moose-hatin’ cousin from Alaska comes to Miami to party at a club with four floors, 13 in-house DJs, and the intimacy of a sardine can, but you have more sense, dear little party animal. You prefer a soiree filled with people who are too cool for McClubs, and even if Club Space promised to have the whole Jackson 5 (with young, black Michael on lead mike) to perform a set with Jay-Z, you’d steer clear. Because they didn’t mention an open bar or drink specials, right? Yah. Well, The Vagabond doesn’t have any specials, but it’s dope enough to be the spot anyway. You can never lose with a grassy back yard fitted with a yummy hot-dog-charring grill. Never. And each Tuesday, jazz, blues, soul, and spoken word take over the spot. They call it Stone Groove. You might have thought hipsters liked only music they could do lines to — such as electronic, dance, and electro-dance — but so not true. They can do lines to anything! And Tuesday night, as long as you’re 21 or older, you can watch and/or participate in the Groove. Open-mike signup starts at 10, so if you want to show off more than your herky-jerky dance moves, that’s your chance to queue up.

You ever want to take a breather from the slick, gay nightlife scene of West Hollywood? You know, skip the lines and cover charges, those anonymous guys you always see at the gym during the week, and the incredibly expensive fancy drinks? Maybe head off into territories unknown or rarely visited? Maybe even meet a new kind of guy? We do all the time. That's why we like to drive over to Silver Lake on a Friday or Saturday for Akbar's "Free Dance" Nights, where you can shimmy on an expanded dance floor and not hear the same music over and over again--either Mike Glass or Jonny Cota will be your DJ for the evening. Akbar, which was named the 2008 "Best Gay Bar" in L.A. Weekly, has always been a welcomed, less self-conscious alternative to Boystown, but some people either forget it's there or don't know exists. But it does exist, and it's calling you. And if you're reading this blurb right now and feel a certain stir in your soul, you must obey it and head over to Akbar immediately. Good things are destined to happen.

Independent rapper Selassie is serious. He wants change -- he's a “revolutionary hip-hop presence,” as he puts it. So what does a man like that do? When you care, and you've read a million books that piss you off, and your neighborhood has problems, someday you have to sit down and think: “What can make a difference in my scene, and thereby in the world -- a practical, quick-acting antidote to violence, despair, and injustice?” (It's not a fun question to ask. Takes a grown-ass person to do it.) And if you stay with the question, you have to take into account who you are personally, and what you have to offer. “I'm not a promoter,” Selassie is careful to point out. But he, along with Gina Gallo of Inhouse Talent, asked the question, and wound up inventing something both simple and powerful. We All We Got is an independent hip-hop showcase, the point being to “Experience a culture of support and success here and now.” Big egos and bad attitudes probably won't be comfortable here, but hard work and big dreams are, he says. (Inhouse Talent also puts on the I'll Play Yo Shit Listening Party; none are scheduled in the Bay Area for a while, but it's a great homegrown idea so keep an eye out.) Tonight's WAWG features Cormega, and past headliners have included Mob Figaz' the Jacka. And who is Selassie? “I’m a self-made 'make something happen-aire.'”

Choreographer Stephen Petronio has amassed a contact list of musicians for which any rock 'n' roll journalist would trade his or her Scotch. The Guggenheim fellow has worked with Lou Reed, Rufus Wainwright, Laurie Anderson, Michael Nyman, James Lavelle, and an ever-growing list of composers and songwriters pushing the boundaries of experimental music. His latest co-conspirator is Radiohead guitarist Jonny Greenwood, the real genius behind the group’s arrangements and just the type of musical mind Petronio finds most complementary. The result of their collaboration is “Ghostown,” a meditation on things that no longer seem to exist but are indeed still a part of the world. After 25 years of forging his own dance style, Petronio has said this latest work marks the beginning of a new type of expressive exploration. Margaret Jenkins has invited Petronio to discuss his new dance narrative and a career arc tonight. Said arc includes pieces such as “#3” (1986), “MiddleSexGorge” (1990), and “Love Me Tender” (1993), which have explored a wide variety of themes and ideas, and secured Petronio’s place in the upper echelon of modern dance choreographers. The talk comes after the March 4 and 5 performances at Yerba Buena Center for the Arts by the Stephen Petronio Company.

“Monster Rally.” Those words usually reside near big metal things with big rubber wheels that jump in the air and crush smaller metal things. They live near big sports arenas and guys in crash helmets, and spectators who wear windbreakers and caps that say things like “USA” and “Built Ford Tough.” They don't often live anywhere near words such as “artist,” “gallery,” or “benefit.” There goes the neighborhood: The Monster Drawing Rally is just what it sounds like — a place where scores of artists gather to make art while hundreds of people gather to watch it being made. Groups of about 30 artists work in one-hour shifts. The spectators walk around and look at what's being created with pencil, charcoal, pen, ink, glitter, marker, paint, and other media. When each shift is over, the drawings are put on the wall and the voyeurs bid on ones they like, starting at $60. There's beer and wine. There's DJ Jason Jagel. And the proceeds go to Southern Exposure, a nonprofit gallery known to be a center for art that's, well, off-center. We can't independently confirm that SoEx was the first to put “Drawing” in the middle of “Monster Rally,” but a couple of similarly named events we found online say they got the idea from the S.F. gallery.

The Cranford High School boys and girls soccer programs, in conjunction with Central Jersey Celtic F.A., present their 2010 Cougar Soccer Camp at Orange Avenue School fields during the week of July 26 through July 30. The camp will run from 9:00am-1:00pm and is open for all boys and girls in grades 1-8, from beginners to advanced.

Camp directors are Cranford boys Head Varsity coach Mike Curci, girls Head Varsity coach Jen Michewitz, and P.J. Keim, President of the Central Jersey F.A.

Curci, honored as 2007 Star-Ledger Coach of the Year in Union County, led the CHS boys' varsity team to the Union County Tournament Championship in 2009, the first in the 54-year history of the program. The Cougars also nailed down their third consecutive Mountain Valley Conference Championship, while posting a record-setting 22-1-2 mark, finishing with a # 7 ranking in the Star-Ledger final Top-20. The 2009 team closed the season at 15-6 despite the loss of seven starters to graduation. The 2008 squad finished 9-1 in conference play, and own a conference record of 28-2 over the last three seasons. The 2007 team also finished with 15 wins while posting the first championship of any kind in the fifty-year history of the program. Over the last two seasons, the Cougars are 52-11-3. Curci, entering his 6th season at CHS, began his coaching career by spending several years as an assistant to the legendary Gene Chyzowych of Columbia High School, the all-time winningest coach in state history. Curci led the Columbia J.V. to a 17-0 mark in his 2nd season there before taking over the varsity program at Livingston H.S. where the Lancers made the state tournament all five years while facing perennial powers Columbia, Seton Hall Prep and St. Benedict's. Curci's playing career includes a conference championship at Carteret High School, before becoming a four-year starter at midfield for Seton Hall University where he led the team in goals his junior season and was named captain his senior season. In Coach C.'s five years at the helm, Cranford has gone from 35 players to 90 student/athletes wearing the white, blue and gold at the varsity, J.V. and freshmen levels. The Cougars look forward to building on their county and conference championship seasons as they continue a tradition of excellence. Mike has called Cranford home for the past 20 years with his wife Sally and their four children.

Michewitz is entering her 3rd season as girls Head Varsity Soccer Coach at Cranford. She guided the Lady Cougars to the Union County Championship in 2009, posting victories over rivals Scotch Plains and Westfield in the final two county games en route to a 16-3 record. Michewitz is a graduate of Seton Hall University where she started on the women's soccer team as a defender all 74 games of her career and was a captain her junior and senior years. In 2002, she received honorable mention for the Freshmen All-American Team, and in 2007 she earned the "Woman of the Year" Award from Seton Hall University for her accomplishments in athletics, academics and community service. Jen grew up in Pottstown, PA where she was highly involved with the Eastern Pennsylvania Soccer Association, training youth teams and coaching soccer camps. She currently lives in Westfield and teaches math at Cranford High School.

PJ Keim is President of  Central Jersey Football Academy, which currently supplies trainers to many of the local soccer clubs. He has been coaching youth soccer for over 12 years. Keim is the head coach of the two-time state cup finalist CWS Red Devils. PJ has lived in Cranford for 18 years and is the father of three wonderful children.

Once again, Mark Dutton, of Central Jersey F.A., will join the camp as Director of Coaching. His goal is to provide a positive and safe learning environment for all ages to become stronger athletes. Mark has been running camps in the U.S. for the past 12 years. Former star CHS players will also be on-hand to share their expertise and skills.

For more information or for a camp brochure, please call Mike Curci at 908-294-2101 or PJ Keim at 908-591-6734, or email mscurci@aol.com. You can also go to www.cjceltic.com to register.

Investigation Destination: Science and Math in Art, is the newest Experiencenter exhibition, opening to the public Thursday, April 8. This exhibition invites visitors to investigate the connections between art and the sciences using three themes: Art that Moves, focusing on the kinetic energy that makes mobiles move, The Geometry of Patterns, focusing on the properties of geometric translations as seen in African textiles and Persian tiles and Keeping Art Ageless,focusing on art conservation and the materials artists use. Each theme is supported by art from the museum's permanent collection along with a site-specific work created by local artist, Terry Welker. Hands-on activities, gallery guides, museum hunts, and take-home activities are also included. The museum has partnered with two schools, Patterson-Kennedy, a Dayton Public School, and the Dayton Regional STEM School and is directly involving students in grades 6-9 and their teachers in the development of the exhibition. The museum is also facilitating activities that are teaching students that the creative innovative skills involved in producing art are the same skills needed by scientists and mathematicians....more

The winter is a wonderful time to see and experience the Wilds at work. Exclusive Winter Safari Tours have been created for adults and children alike to experience the Wilds between the general visitor seasons. See and learn about rare and endangered animals during the winter months of November through March on these special safari tour programs. The Winter Safari Tours begin with a light lunch and short conservation program presented by an experienced program staff member. After lunch, visitors board a heated Safari Transport for a guided safari tour experience through the winter landscape. View large groups of animals, such as the Sichuan takin, Pere David's deer, Przewalski's wild horse, American bison, and many more, as they roam in the open pasture in their winter coats. A Reasonable Facsimile

Christensen Center Art Gallery
January 10 – February 25, 2011

In the midst of the millions of text messages sent each day, a group of twelve photographers took eight months to play a visual game of telephone using the U.S. Postal Service. The curator of the project, Michelle Westmark, began the photo chain by sending a 4"x 6" postcard version of her image to be interpreted by the next photographer on the list. This artist had a two-week window to photographically respond to the image's subject, content or formal elements and pass a postcard of the new image along, creating a visual and tactile conversation that progressed around the country. While so much of our globally digitalized world speeds along, A Reasonable Facsimile pauses to find connections within a variety of locations and lenses.

Photographers included in the exhibition are Michelle Westmark (MN), Conor King (CO), Lindsay Borden (WA), Sarah Christianson (CA), Yasmin Etemadi (CA), Sarah Baron (NC), Sarah Stacke (NY), Salma Khalil (DE), Rachel Loischild (MA), Jason Flack (MA), Carl Sweets (IL), and Brett Kallusky (MN).

Michelle Westmark received her B.A. from Bethel University and her M.F.A. from Pratt Institute where she studied photography.  She is currently the Gallery Director and an Assistant Professor of Art at Bethel University.

Force of Luminosity, an exhibition of new landscape paintings by Minneapolis artist James Conaway opens January 21 at the Groveland Annex.

Conaway, a former Hamline University professor, taught studio art and art history for over three decades. He is now a full-time artist with a studio in the Minneapolis warehouse district. He has been represented by Groveland Gallery for over 11 years, and has exhibited his work extensively throughout the United States, including the Walker Art Center, the Milwaukee Art Museum, and the Scottsdale Center for the Arts.

Conaway is an avid world-traveler, and his paintings draw upon the varied landscapes he has visited during his travels. His interest in topography, season, and light provides a rich combination for his painterly, pastoral scenes: golden, autumnal pastures, sky-blue rivers beneath pinky sunrises and tree groves casting shadows on ruddy hillsides. His idealized landscapes, often painted on old, weathered pieces of wood, create a unique dialogue between the imagined trees of his painted forests and the weighty material on which he is painting. Though his landscapes do not depict real places, they are rooted in Conaway’s real experiences of the land, water, and skies in Minnesota and beyond.

The artist will be present at the opening reception on Friday, January 21 from 5-8 p.m. The exhibition runs concurrently with Presence, an exhibition by Joyce Lyons and Carl Oltvedt in the main gallery.

Groveland Gallery is pleased to announce an exhibition of new drawings by Minnesota artists Joyce Lyon and Carl Oltvedt. Oltvedt and Lyon approach their plein-air landscape drawings in a similar manner. For each of these artists, the process of drawing is as important as the drawing itself – “translating experience into drawing,” as Lyon explains. Capturing the “feeling” of a place through carefully composed compositions and the subtleties of line lends a quiet intensity to Lyon’s haunting groves of twisted olive trees and Oltvedt’s soft, dewy pastures.

Lyon, a New York native and an associate professor at the University of Minnesota, was a founding member of the Women’s Art Registry of Minnesota (WARM). She is the recipient of three Minnesota State Arts Board Fellowships, as well as a Jerome/MCBA grant. Her work is in public and private collections nationally, including the Florida Holocaust Museum, the Minneapolis Institute of Arts, the Walker Art Center, and the Weisman Art Museum.

A Minneapolis native, Carl Oltvedt is a professor at Minnesota State University at Moorhead, where he has taught for nearly 30 years. His work is included in the permanent collections of the Honolulu Academy of Arts, the North Dakota Museum of Art, the Minnesota Museum of American Art, the Minneapolis Institute of Art, the Minnesota State Historical Society, and the Plains Art Museum.

The artists will be present at the opening reception Friday, January 21 from 5-8 p.m. This opening reception and exhibition run concurrently with the exhibition in the Groveland Annex, Force of Luminosity, by James Conaway.

Leaving aside the issue of grants and funding, maybe our current recession could be a good thing for the arts. Or at least for sites and venues owned by developers who can’t raise the money to raze or build on them. Look around Seattle, and you’ll see a lot of empty storefronts. Or as I envision them: future exhibition spaces. That’s the notion, too, at Burien Town Square, where planned condo construction has been delayed on a one-acre parking lot. There, for the next year, will sprout the Burien Interim Art Space, an outdoor sculpture garden being seeded with five large pieces this week. In the future, say Kathy Justin and Dane Johnson, they hope more art and events will be added through community participation. For now, after a year’s volunteer effort, the two are acting as curators-with-a-backhoe, literally tearing up the pavement to create earthen pads for the sculptures. Most prominent among them will be the 30-foot-tall The Passage, by Dan Das Mann and Karen Cusolito, comprised of a five- and three-ton metal mother-and-child array (previously seen at Burning Man ’05). After being trucked up from Oakland, it’ll be hoisted into place Thursday by the condo builders next door. (A good partner to have in the joint venture, which also includes the City of Burien, expected to open its new city hall/library at the four-block, mixed-use Burien Town Square this April, with more arts events planned.) Says Burien resident Johnson, “Seattle has its Olympic Sculpture Garden for its art superstars,” while this will be more DIY and inclusive. “There will be no ‘Don’t touch the art’ signs,” he adds. Fire performers, dancers, and music will attend the (snow-delayed) grand opening. After that, artists, new art, and volunteers are welcome. BRIAN MILLER

Since opening last year, the Olympic Sculpture Park has somehow eclipsed and subsumed the identity of Myrtle Edwards Park, which was established (with a different name) back in 1964, when SAM was still a small institution confined to Capitol Hill. The narrow old shoreline park was renamed in 1976 for the pioneering city councilwoman (1894–1969), and public art has been added at various junctures. Walk north of the OSP and you’ll find Michael Heizer’s Adjacent, Against, Upon(1976), which creates a grammar between three giant concrete slabs, obviously manmade, and three corresponding granite boulders (quarried from the Cascades and delivered by barge). The work is a series of prepositions running south to north, a delicate dance of heavyweights that tip the scales between 30 and 50 tons. Back in ’76, when the project was funded by the NEA, City Light, Virginia Wright, and the Seattle Arts Commission, it was “initially controversial,” according to the city Web site. Why controversial? I recall happily climbing on the rocks as a kid. But today I can imagine what might be called the Richard Serra Effect—it’s too big, too unfriendly, too invasive! It’s not a statue with a noble or smiling face (remember that patriotic bicentennial year). Three decades later, surrounded by well-tended gravel, the installation holds up remarkably well. Visitors picnic upon the rocks (or adjacent, or against); tourists pose with it; and unlike your snooty OSP, there’s no prohibition against touching or climbing on the things. Each smooth slab is a foundation. Each roughhewn boulder lies in a position of order or disorder, depending on which direction you walk past. The work either illustrates entropy or acts despite it. It was also reportedly the first public commission for Heizer (then 32), who for the past few decades has been remaking a big patch of Nevada desert into City, already considered one of America’s most significant examples of environmental art. (He’s continuing the tradition of his late friend and colleague Robert Smithson, famed for Spiral Jetty.) Adjacent, Against, Upon is a comparatively small-scale work in Heizer’s catalog; if it once seemed massive to Seattle pedestrians, it now reminds us how much larger the city has grown. BRIAN MILLER

It’s the day you’ve been waiting for. Your closest family and friends are gathered, sun-drenched in their finest, inhaling the sweet fragrance of the twin rows of rose bushes. The flower girl, her bow tied just so, swings her petal-filled basket. In the distance, the majestic Olympics hold vigil over the deep, sparkling waters of Elliott Bay, onto which a fireboat shoots a multi-streamed fountain salute. Yet on this, your wedding day, you feel a certain energy welling up within you. Sure, you’re all dressed up. But that’s nothing. To your left are the chin-up bars, the dip bars, the sit-up station, with its green enamel grating and shiny black foothold. And, of course, in the dirt: That rusted old iron dumbell, chained to the wooden pole, its two bulbous ends connected for eternity. A sweet foreboding. It calls you. And you answer. Just ten reps. Just the tip. This is why you chose the Rose Garden at Elliott Bay Park (at Pier 86 at the northern edge of Myrtle Edwards). DAMON AGNOS

Royal Purple Raceway benefits from incredible atmospheric conditions because of its proximity to Trinity Bay, which feeds the facility cool air. The track’s first NHRA national event, in fall 1988, established RPR as one of the sport’s quickest with NHRA’s first four-second Top Fuel quarter-mile pass and a new national record. Since then, the track has hosted a dizzying array of record runs, including the first sub-4.5-second Top Fuel quarter-mile pass by Larry Dixon in 1999. Pro Stock Motorcycles and Pro Mods will also compete at the event.
 
2010 recap: Matt Hagan’s first Funny Car win and Larry Dixon’s 50th in Top Fuel highlighted a spectacular race day. Jeg Coughlin Jr. and Andrew Hines earned respective wins in Pro Stock and Pro Stock Motorcycle. From the opening round of Top Fuel through the final rounds, the day was filled with intense action, wild races, and upsets aplenty.
 
How to Get There: Baytown is about 25 miles east of downtown Houston. From downtown Houston, take I-10 east to SH 99 Grand Parkway (Exit 799) and go south to FM 565 (approximately 2 miles). Take FM 565 west (right), and the track is on the right.
 
Visitor Information: Baytown Chamber of Commerce, 281-422-8359

Radio Frequency: 96.7 FM
 
One of NHRA’s long-established events — the race celebrated its 30th anniversary last season — this belle of the South has gained a reputation as one of the tougher events on the tour to win. With summer approaching, warm temperatures can turn the event into “Hotlanta” and throw crew chiefs a curve as they try to glue their charges to the facility’s 660-foot concrete launchpad. The event also includes Pro Stock Motorcycles and Pro Mods.
 
2010 recap: Larry Dixon in Top Fuel and Jeg Coughlin Jr. in Pro Stock scored very special wins and were joined in victory by Robert Hight (Funny Car) and Andrew Hines (Pro Stock Motorcycle). Coughlin’s win was the 50th of his Pro Stock career, making him just the ninth driver to collect 50 Wallys in a Full Throttle class, and Dixon’s 52nd victory tied him in class wins with the great Joe Amato. Although the incoming points leaders left with their leads intact — and, in Dixon’s case, improved — plenty of shuffling occurred behind them.
 
How to Get There: The track is about 65 miles north of Atlanta on Interstate 85 at U.S. Highway 441. From Atlanta, take I-85 north to Exit 149 (Highway 441). Travel north on Highway 441 to Steven Tanger Boulevard. Go left on Tanger Boulevard, then right on E. Ridgeway Road, and follow the signs to the track (approximately a half-mile on the right).
 
Visitor Information: Atlanta Dragway, 706-335-2301; Banks County Chamber of Commerce, 706-677-2108; Banks County Convention and Visitors Bureau, 706-677-5265

Sprawling multipurpose Heartland Park Topeka has been a Midwest favorite since it opened in 1989, but its dragstrip has gained the majority of headlines. The event, originally in the fall, has featured numerous record performances, the most significant of which was the shattering of the quarter-mile four-second and 300-mph barriers in Funny Car in 1993. The event moved to its current spot on the schedule in 2001.
2010 recap: Reigning NHRA Full Throttle Drag Racing Series world champs Tony Schumacher (Top Fuel), Robert Hight (Funny Car), and Mike Edwards (Pro Stock) collected wins to bolster their title defenses. Neither Schumacher nor Hight had won in Topeka, but both crossed that task off their lists to move closer to the points leaders in their classes. Edwards, meanwhile, upped his already impressive points lead to 267 markers over runner-up Allen Johnson.
 
How to Get There: The track is on Topeka Boulevard where it intersects Gary Ormsby Drive, four miles south of Interstate 470. From Kansas City, take the Kansas Turnpike (I-70) to the South Topeka exit and travel south on Topeka Boulevard to the track. From Wichita, take the Kansas Turnpike (I-335) to the South Topeka exit and travel south on Topeka Boulevard to the track. From I-470, take the Topeka Boulevard exit and travel south to the track.
 
Visitor Information: Visit Topeka Inc., 785-234-1030 or 800-235-1030, www.visittopeka.travel

One of NHRA’s original seven national events, this race is steeped in legend: a historic facility, some of the sport’s more knowledgeable fans, and a score of dramatic moments. The event, once known as the Summernationals, has shifted on the schedule from its original scorching hot and humid July slot to May and June, and upsets have become the norm. The event, which marks the midpoint of the Full Throttle regular season, also includes Pro Stock Motorcycles and Pro Mods.
 
2010 recap: Larry Dixon, Bob Tasca III, Mike Edwards, and Michael Phillips claimed Monday victories at the rain-delayed event. Top Fuel finalists Dixon and Antron Brown had shared the Old Bridge winner’s circle before, in 2005 when Dixon won his third of five Top Fuel titles here and Brown the second of his Pro Stock Motorcycle event crowns. This time, though, Dixon went to the trophy presentation solo after winning the rematch of the 2009 final.
 
How to Get There: Englishtown is about 20 miles south of Newark Int’l Airport, 35 miles south of New York City, and 55 miles north of Philadelphia. The track is on Pension Road, two miles north of Englishtown. From the New Jersey Turnpike, use Exit 8 (Route 33) or Exit 9 (Route 18). From Route 33, travel east to Route 527 (Englishtown exit), then north to the track. From Route 18, travel east to Route 527 (Englishtown exit), then south to the track. The main entrance is on Pension Road, which runs off Route 527 west of the track.
 
Visitor Information: Old Bridge Township Raceway Park, 732-446-7800, www.racewaypark.com

Bristol Dragway is known as Thunder Valley not only because it cuts a path between mountains but also because it can be home to incredible performances. The facility hosted NHRA’s Springnationals from 1965 to 1967 and non-NHRA events until it was closed in 1996 for an $18 million renovation. It reopened in 1999 and was the site of NHRA’s all-star event that year and in 2000 before hosting its first national event in 34 years in 2001. The event is the final chance for Pro Stock teams to earn points toward making the field for the K&N Horsepower Challenge and another stop on the tour for Pro Mod racers.
 
2010 recap: Tony Schumacher (Top Fuel), John Force (Funny Car), and Mike Edwards (Pro Stock) collected victories at an event that produced a new points leader in Funny Car, a substantially tighter battle in Top Fuel, and additions to the all-important top 10s as the regular season headed down the backstretch. Force, the early season points leader, hadn’t been to a final round since winning in Las Vegas in April and not only got back to the winner’s circle but also got back his points lead.
 
How to Get There: Bristol Dragway’s Thunder Valley is on Highway 394. From the south, exit Interstate 81 at Tennessee Exit 69, then travel east on Highway 394. From the north, exit Interstate 81 at Virginia Exit 17 and take Virginia State Route 75 south to Tennessee 44 south to U.S. 421 north to Highway 394 south; or exit Interstate 81 at Virginia Exit 3 and take Highway 11E south to Highway 394.
 
Visitor Information: Bristol Chamber of Commerce, 423-989-4850

Actress and comedian Sue Costello, a native of Boston, has had her own self-titled Fox sitcom, appeared in several hit movies, and performed her stand-up on Last Comic Standing. Our Man is a comedic multidisciplinary performance work that explores the intersection of performance and politics in the modern age, through the lenses of 1950’s era radio broadcasts, and a decidedly fictional approach to American political history. Two men in a small glass box are tasked with narrating the life and accomplishments of one of the nations most controversial leaders, “The Gipper”. Forced to perform the same radio play over and over again for an invisible audience, the lines of fact and fiction blur as the men begin to slowly re-write the course of history in an effort to entertain each other and
understand the context of their unusual situation. Through clever and hilarious half truths and brutal mudslinging tactics, the two find themselves arguing their way through small towns in the Midwest, all the way to Europe on the front lines of WWII, all the while deciding whether or not to elect their only possession, an old wooden tennis racquet, their President.

Our Man is conceived and performed by GRP’s William Bowling and Christopher Kaminstein, and is written by the duo and collaborator Sascha Stanton-Craven.

Goat In The Road is a young, New Orleans based performance ensemble, dedicated to the production of original and invigorating new works or theatre, dance, performance art, and educational programming. Their work has been presented at the New Orleans Fringe Festival in 2008 (Calculus of Hope) and 2009 (Major Swelling Salvation Salve Medicine Show) and in other theaters and site-specific locations around New Orleans.

The 44th season opens June 23-26 with the classic, Man of La Mancha (book by Dale Wasserman, music by Mitch Leigh, and lyrics by Joe Darion). Man of La Mancha tells the story of Miguel de Cervantes. He is aging and an utter failure in his varied careers as playwright, poet and tax collector for the government and has been thrown into a dungeon in Seville to await trial by the Inquisition for an offense against the Church. Thus begins the journey that is Man of La Mancha – a remarkable show and one of the great theatre successes of our time having been revived four times on Broadway. This multi Tony award-winning musical is a play-within-a-play, based on Cervantes’ Don Quixote. We have a poignant story of a dying old man whose impossible dream takes over his mind. His dream is Everyman’s dream. His tilting at windmills is Everyman’s great adventure. Somehow, the footlights disappear, time is telescoped and the Man of La Mancha speaks for humankind. “It’s All the Same,” “Dulcinea,” “I’m Only Thinking of Him,” “I Really Like Him,” “Little Bird,” and “The Impossible Dream” remain in your thoughts and in your soul well after you experience the performance.

James Lapine and Stephen Sondheim’s multi Tony award-winning fractured fairy tale, Into the Woods, opens as the season’s second production from July 14 -17. An ambivalent Cinderella? A blood-thirsty Little Red Ridinghood? A Prince Charming with a roving eye? A Witch…who raps? They’re all among the cockeyed characters in Into the Woods. When a Baker and his Wife learn they’ve been cursed with childlessness by the Witch next door, they embark on a quest for the special objects required to break the spell, swindling, lying to and stealing from Cinderella, Little Red, Rapunzel and Jack (the one who climbed the beanstalk). Everyone’s wish is granted at the end of Act One, but the consequences of their actions return to haunt them later, with disastrous results. What begins as a lively irreverent fantasy becomes a moving lesson about community responsibility and the stories we tell our children. Thought-provoking and memorable songs such as “Into the Woods,” “No One Is Alone,” and “Children Will Listen” beckon you. So by all means, go to Into the Woods. Admire the view. But above all, listen.

6 WICKEDLY FUNNY ONE-ACTS - All in the Timing is a collection of  comic one acts by David Ives.  Ives, a native of  Chicago is one of Americas' premier playwrights working in short form.  David Ives's six short plays that comprise All in the Timing are built on snappy patter, quick-fire timing,  inspired gibberish and paradoxical plot quirks, and it takes a quick-witted and nimble audience to keep up with Mr. Ives' unique take of the universe.  Crown City Theatre is using 2 different directors each tackling 3 one acts apiece to keep up with the merriment.

This show explores the world of four older gay men who are unhealthily obsessed with the famous foursome. Thanks to their equally dysfunctional therapist, they are able to explore their obsession through a novel new therapy. Through the process, they are also able to search their shallow souls for answers to other questions facing older gay men, the answers often coming in the form of a show tune from the decades familiar to thirty-somethings and above.    The neighborhood is full of nightspots for before Theatre dining and after Theatre libations.    Widestance Productions first brought these men who resemble women to life in September of 2009 with quick comeback in Los Angeles in January so they could tune up to take the show to larger venues in Palm Springs and Miami. The show received accolades from critics and the Public alike and was a BroadwayWorld.com People’s Choice Award winner in two categories (best ensemble, best new work). All previous performances were sold out. This show, originally written over ten years ago has shed a character and a few unneeded lines for this new rendering. This version will be directed by Sean Riley and the Musical Director is Anthony Starble.

An epic true story set against the backdrop of one of the wildest places on Earth, African Cats captures the real-life love, humor and determination of the majestic kings of the savanna. Disneynature brings “The Lion King” to life on the big screen in this True Life Adventure directed by Keith Scholey and Alastair Fothergill (“Earth”). Based on Puccini's 'La Boheme', Jonathan Larsons Tony Award and Pulitzer Prize-winning revolutionary rock opera Rent tells the story of one year in the life of eight friends living the Bohemian life struggling to express themselves through their art and measuring their lives in love. Against the gritty backdrop of New Yorks East Village, these friends strive for success and acceptance while enduring the obstacles of poverty, illness and the AIDS epidemic.

Directed by Jerianne Banson, featuring Enrico Banson, Marion Bordon, Luke Chapman, Jenna Davi, Corinne Frimbrez, Jami James, Anthony Michael Knott, Jessica Knudsen, Chris Morell, Salvador Real, Ruben Oriol Rivera, Alex Rodriguez, Anthony Rollins-Mullens, Jujuana Williams, and Aubine Nicole Wise.

RENT runs January 21, 22, 34, 2010 at 8pm, and January 23 and 24, 2010 at 2pm at The Southside Theatre  Fort Mason Center, Building D  in San Francisco. Tickets are $25-$35, and are available by visiting the Jerica Productions website at http://www.jericaproductions.com.

During the past 20 years, Chico MacMurtrie's kinetic, monumental sculputral installations have focused on different representations of the body -- both human and animal. 


Expanding and contracting in various configurations, the sculptures developed for the Beall Center exhibition are controlled by computational methods.  Using the principles of a skeletal-muscular system powered by compressed air, MacMurtrie's objects oscillate, creating the illusion of living objects.  MacMurtrie's work dynamically responds to the movements of its viewers to create a menagerie of moving forms.


Exhibition organized by David Familian, Beall Center Artistic Director

Christensen Center Art Gallery

To determine the schema integration, I will analyze the attributes of the source table to identify distinct entity types.

**1. Identify Entity Types:**
Looking at the columns, we can group them into logical concepts:
*   **Event Details:** `name`, `description`, `allDates` (start date), `endDate`, `price`. These describe the specific occurrence or listing of an event.
*   **Venue Details:** `venueName`, `address`, `city`, `state`, `zipcode`, `latitude`, `longitude`. These describe the physical location where the event takes place.
*   **Contact/Organization Details:** `phone`, `email`, `website`, `moreInfoLink`, `image`. These describe how to contact the organizer or find more info. Note that `phone` and `email` are often associated with the venue or the specific event organizer, but `website` and `moreInfoLink` are strongly tied to the event listing or the venue.

**2. Choose Main Entity:**
The table primarily lists **Events**. The `name` column contains event names (e.g., "Bachata: DJ Alison", "Film Fundrager!"). The `allDates` and `endDate` are specific to the event instance. Therefore, "Event" is the main entity.

**3. Identify Related Entities:**
*   **Venue:** The location where the event happens. Attributes: `venueName`, `address`, `city`, `state`, `zipcode`, `latitude`, `longitude`.
*   **Contact/Info:** Information about the event or its organizer. Attributes: `phone`, `email`, `website`, `moreInfoLink`, `image`.

**4. Assign Attributes:**

*   **Event Entity:**
    *   `name`: Name of the event.
    *   `description`: Details about the event.
    *   `allDates`: Start date(s).
    *   `endDate`: End date.
    *   `price`: Cost of entry.
    *   *Note:* `phone`, `email`, `website`, `moreInfoLink`, `image` could arguably belong to the event or the organizer. However, `website` and `moreInfoLink` are very specific to the event listing. `phone` and `email` are ambiguous (venue vs organizer). Let's look at the data.
        *   Row 1: Phone is present, Venue is HaLo.
        *   Row 2: No phone, No venue name.
        *   Row 5: Phone is present, Venue is Bainbridge Performing Arts.
    *   It is common in such flat tables for contact info to be associated with the *Event* listing if the venue doesn't have a dedicated phone listed separately, or if the event organizer is different from the venue. However, `website` and `moreInfoLink` are definitely event-specific. `image` is event-specific.
    *   Let's group `phone`, `email`, `website`, `moreInfoLink`, `image` into a "Contact" or "EventDetails" group? Or keep them with Event?
    *   Let's look at the Venue group: `venueName`, `address`, `city`, `state`, `zipcode`, `latitude`, `longitude`. This is a very strong, cohesive group (7 attributes).
    *   The remaining attributes are: `name`, `description`, `allDates`, `endDate`, `price`, `phone`, `email`, `website`, `moreInfoLink`, `image`.
    *   If we split Venue out, the Event table still has 10 attributes.
    *   Is there a third entity? "Organizer"? We don't have an organizer name. We have `phone` and `email`.
    *   Let's check the overlap.
        *   Venue attributes: `venueName`, `address`, `city`, `state`, `zipcode`, `latitude`, `longitude`.
        *   Event attributes: `name`, `description`, `allDates`, `endDate`, `price`.
        *   Contact/Web attributes: `phone`, `email`, `website`, `moreInfoLink`, `image`.

    Let's evaluate splitting into **Event**, **Venue**, and **ContactInfo**.
    
    *   **Venue Table:** `venueName`, `address`, `city`, `state`, `zipcode`, `latitude`, `longitude`. (7 attributes). This is a valid table.
    *   **Event Table:** `name`, `description`, `allDates`, `endDate`, `price`. (5 attributes). This is a valid table.
    *   **ContactInfo Table:** `phone`, `email`, `website`, `moreInfoLink`, `image`. (5 attributes). This is a valid table.

    However, `phone` and `email` are often associated with the *Venue* in real-world schemas, or the *Event Organizer*. In this specific dataset:
    *   Row 1: Phone `(206)...` is likely the venue (HaLo) or the DJ.
    *   Row 5: Phone `206-842-1163` is likely the venue (Bainbridge Performing Arts).
    
    If I assign `phone` and `email` to **Venue**, the Venue table becomes: `venueName`, `address`, `city`, `state`, `zipcode`, `latitude`, `longitude`, `phone`, `email`. (9 attributes).
    Then **Event** table: `name`, `description`, `allDates`, `endDate`, `price`, `website`, `moreInfoLink`, `image`. (8 attributes).
    
    This seems like a more natural semantic split:
    1.  **Venue**: Physical location and its contact info.
    2.  **Event**: The happening, its schedule, cost, and online presence (website/image).

    Let's check if `website` and `moreInfoLink` belong to Venue or Event.
    *   Row 1: Website `http://www.thestranger.com...` is an article about the event/location.
    *   Row 2: Website `http://philly.cities2night.com...` is the event page.
    *   Row 5: Website `http://www.bainbridgeperformingarts.org...` is the venue's education page.
    
    It's mixed. `moreInfoLink` is definitely event-specific (links to the specific event listing). `website` is ambiguous. `image` is usually event-specific (poster for the event).
    
    Let's stick to the strongest semantic clusters:
    *   **Cluster 1 (Location):** `venueName`, `address`, `city`, `state`, `zipcode`, `latitude`, `longitude`.
    *   **Cluster 2 (Event Core):** `name`, `description`, `allDates`, `endDate`, `price`.
    *   **Cluster 3 (Digital/Contact):** `phone`, `email`, `website`, `moreInfoLink`, `image`.

    If I split into 3 tables:
    1.  `venue`: `venueName`, `address`, `city`, `state`, `zipcode`, `latitude`, `longitude`

Your moose-hatin’ cousin from Alaska comes to Miami to party at a club with four floors, 13 in-house DJs, and the intimacy of a sardine can, but you have more sense, dear little party animal. You prefer a soiree filled with people who are too cool for McClubs, and even if Club Space promised to have the whole Jackson 5 (with young, black Michael on lead mike) to perform a set with Jay-Z, you’d steer clear. Because they didn’t mention an open bar or drink specials, right? Yah. Well, The Vagabond doesn’t have any specials, but it’s dope enough to be the spot anyway. You can never lose with a grassy back yard fitted with a yummy hot-dog-charring grill. Never. And each Tuesday, jazz, blues, soul, and spoken word take over the spot. They call it Stone Groove. You might have thought hipsters liked only music they could do lines to — such as electronic, dance, and electro-dance — but so not true. They can do lines to anything! And Tuesday night, as long as you’re 21 or older, you can watch and/or participate in the Groove. Open-mike signup starts at 10, so if you want to show off more than your herky-jerky dance moves, that’s your chance to queue up.

You ever want to take a breather from the slick, gay nightlife scene of West Hollywood? You know, skip the lines and cover charges, those anonymous guys you always see at the gym during the week, and the incredibly expensive fancy drinks? Maybe head off into territories unknown or rarely visited? Maybe even meet a new kind of guy? We do all the time. That's why we like to drive over to Silver Lake on a Friday or Saturday for Akbar's "Free Dance" Nights, where you can shimmy on an expanded dance floor and not hear the same music over and over again--either Mike Glass or Jonny Cota will be your DJ for the evening. Akbar, which was named the 2008 "Best Gay Bar" in L.A. Weekly, has always been a welcomed, less self-conscious alternative to Boystown, but some people either forget it's there or don't know exists. But it does exist, and it's calling you. And if you're reading this blurb right now and feel a certain stir in your soul, you must obey it and head over to Akbar immediately. Good things are destined to happen.

Independent rapper Selassie is serious. He wants change -- he's a “revolutionary hip-hop presence,” as he puts it. So what does a man like that do? When you care, and you've read a million books that piss you off, and your neighborhood has problems, someday you have to sit down and think: “What can make a difference in my scene, and thereby in the world -- a practical, quick-acting antidote to violence, despair, and injustice?” (It's not a fun question to ask. Takes a grown-ass person to do it.) And if you stay with the question, you have to take into account who you are personally, and what you have to offer. “I'm not a promoter,” Selassie is careful to point out. But he, along with Gina Gallo of Inhouse Talent, asked the question, and wound up inventing something both simple and powerful. We All We Got is an independent hip-hop showcase, the point being to “Experience a culture of support and success here and now.” Big egos and bad attitudes probably won't be comfortable here, but hard work and big dreams are, he says. (Inhouse Talent also puts on the I'll Play Yo Shit Listening Party; none are scheduled in the Bay Area for a while, but it's a great homegrown idea so keep an eye out.) Tonight's WAWG features Cormega, and past headliners have included Mob Figaz' the Jacka. And who is Selassie? “I’m a self-made 'make something happen-aire.'”

Choreographer Stephen Petronio has amassed a contact list of musicians for which any rock 'n' roll journalist would trade his or her Scotch. The Guggenheim fellow has worked with Lou Reed, Rufus Wainwright, Laurie Anderson, Michael Nyman, James Lavelle, and an ever-growing list of composers and songwriters pushing the boundaries of experimental music. His latest co-conspirator is Radiohead guitarist Jonny Greenwood, the real genius behind the group’s arrangements and just the type of musical mind Petronio finds most complementary. The result of their collaboration is “Ghostown,” a meditation on things that no longer seem to exist but are indeed still a part of the world. After 25 years of forging his own dance style, Petronio has said this latest work marks the beginning of a new type of expressive exploration. Margaret Jenkins has invited Petronio to discuss his new dance narrative and a career arc tonight. Said arc includes pieces such as “#3” (1986), “MiddleSexGorge” (1990), and “Love Me Tender” (1993), which have explored a wide variety of themes and ideas, and secured Petronio’s place in the upper echelon of modern dance choreographers. The talk comes after the March 4 and 5 performances at Yerba Buena Center for the Arts by the Stephen Petronio Company.

“Monster Rally.” Those words usually reside near big metal things with big rubber wheels that jump in the air and crush smaller metal things. They live near big sports arenas and guys in crash helmets, and spectators who wear windbreakers and caps that say things like “USA” and “Built Ford Tough.” They don't often live anywhere near words such as “artist,” “gallery,” or “benefit.” There goes the neighborhood: The Monster Drawing Rally is just what it sounds like — a place where scores of artists gather to make art while hundreds of people gather to watch it being made. Groups of about 30 artists work in one-hour shifts. The spectators walk around and look at what's being created with pencil, charcoal, pen, ink, glitter, marker, paint, and other media. When each shift is over, the drawings are put on the wall and the voyeurs bid on ones they like, starting at $60. There's beer and wine. There's DJ Jason Jagel. And the proceeds go to Southern Exposure, a nonprofit gallery known to be a center for art that's, well, off-center. We can't independently confirm that SoEx was the first to put “Drawing” in the middle of “Monster Rally,” but a couple of similarly named events we found online say they got the idea from the S.F. gallery.

Investigation Destination: Science and Math in Art, is the newest Experiencenter exhibition, opening to the public Thursday, April 8. This exhibition invites visitors to investigate the connections between art and the sciences using three themes: Art that Moves, focusing on the kinetic energy that makes mobiles move, The Geometry of Patterns, focusing on the properties of geometric translations as seen in African textiles and Persian tiles and Keeping Art Ageless,focusing on art conservation and the materials artists use. Each theme is supported by art from the museum's permanent collection along with a site-specific work created by local artist, Terry Welker. Hands-on activities, gallery guides, museum hunts, and take-home activities are also included. The museum has partnered with two schools, Patterson-Kennedy, a Dayton Public School, and the Dayton Regional STEM School and is directly involving students in grades 6-9 and their teachers in the development of the exhibition. The museum is also facilitating activities that are teaching students that the creative innovative skills involved in producing art are the same skills needed by scientists and mathematicians....more

A Reasonable Facsimile

Christensen Center Art Gallery
January 10 – February 25, 2011

In the midst of the millions of text messages sent each day, a group of twelve photographers took eight months to play a visual game of telephone using the U.S. Postal Service. The curator of the project, Michelle Westmark, began the photo chain by sending a 4"x 6" postcard version of her image to be interpreted by the next photographer on the list. This artist had a two-week window to photographically respond to the image's subject, content or formal elements and pass a postcard of the new image along, creating a visual and tactile conversation that progressed around the country. While so much of our globally digitalized world speeds along, A Reasonable Facsimile pauses to find connections within a variety of locations and lenses.

Photographers included in the exhibition are Michelle Westmark (MN), Conor King (CO), Lindsay Borden (WA), Sarah Christianson (CA), Yasmin Etemadi (CA), Sarah Baron (NC), Sarah Stacke (NY), Salma Khalil (DE), Rachel Loischild (MA), Jason Flack (MA), Carl Sweets (IL), and Brett Kallusky (MN).

Michelle Westmark received her B.A. from Bethel University and her M.F.A. from Pratt Institute where she studied photography.  She is currently the Gallery Director and an Assistant Professor of Art at Bethel University.

Force of Luminosity, an exhibition of new landscape paintings by Minneapolis artist James Conaway opens January 21 at the Groveland Annex.

Conaway, a former Hamline University professor, taught studio art and art history for over three decades. He is now a full-time artist with a studio in the Minneapolis warehouse district. He has been represented by Groveland Gallery for over 11 years, and has exhibited his work extensively throughout the United States, including the Walker Art Center, the Milwaukee Art Museum, and the Scottsdale Center for the Arts.

Conaway is an avid world-traveler, and his paintings draw upon the varied landscapes he has visited during his travels. His interest in topography, season, and light provides a rich combination for his painterly, pastoral scenes: golden, autumnal pastures, sky-blue rivers beneath pinky sunrises and tree groves casting shadows on ruddy hillsides. His idealized landscapes, often painted on old, weathered pieces of wood, create a unique dialogue between the imagined trees of his painted forests and the weighty material on which he is painting. Though his landscapes do not depict real places, they are rooted in Conaway’s real experiences of the land, water, and skies in Minnesota and beyond.

The artist will be present at the opening reception on Friday, January 21 from 5-8 p.m. The exhibition runs concurrently with Presence, an exhibition by Joyce Lyons and Carl Oltvedt in the main gallery.

Groveland Gallery is pleased to announce an exhibition of new drawings by Minnesota artists Joyce Lyon and Carl Oltvedt. Oltvedt and Lyon approach their plein-air landscape drawings in a similar manner. For each of these artists, the process of drawing is as important as the drawing itself – “translating experience into drawing,” as Lyon explains. Capturing the “feeling” of a place through carefully composed compositions and the subtleties of line lends a quiet intensity to Lyon’s haunting groves of twisted olive trees and Oltvedt’s soft, dewy pastures.

Lyon, a New York native and an associate professor at the University of Minnesota, was a founding member of the Women’s Art Registry of Minnesota (WARM). She is the recipient of three Minnesota State Arts Board Fellowships, as well as a Jerome/MCBA grant. Her work is in public and private collections nationally, including the Florida Holocaust Museum, the Minneapolis Institute of Arts, the Walker Art Center, and the Weisman Art Museum.

A Minneapolis native, Carl Oltvedt is a professor at Minnesota State University at Moorhead, where he has taught for nearly 30 years. His work is included in the permanent collections of the Honolulu Academy of Arts, the North Dakota Museum of Art, the Minnesota Museum of American Art, the Minneapolis Institute of Art, the Minnesota State Historical Society, and the Plains Art Museum.

The artists will be present at the opening reception Friday, January 21 from 5-8 p.m. This opening reception and exhibition run concurrently with the exhibition in the Groveland Annex, Force of Luminosity, by James Conaway.

Leaving aside the issue of grants and funding, maybe our current recession could be a good thing for the arts. Or at least for sites and venues owned by developers who can’t raise the money to raze or build on them. Look around Seattle, and you’ll see a lot of empty storefronts. Or as I envision them: future exhibition spaces. That’s the notion, too, at Burien Town Square, where planned condo construction has been delayed on a one-acre parking lot. There, for the next year, will sprout the Burien Interim Art Space, an outdoor sculpture garden being seeded with five large pieces this week. In the future, say Kathy Justin and Dane Johnson, they hope more art and events will be added through community participation. For now, after a year’s volunteer effort, the two are acting as curators-with-a-backhoe, literally tearing up the pavement to create earthen pads for the sculptures. Most prominent among them will be the 30-foot-tall The Passage, by Dan Das Mann and Karen Cusolito, comprised of a five- and three-ton metal mother-and-child array (previously seen at Burning Man ’05). After being trucked up from Oakland, it’ll be hoisted into place Thursday by the condo builders next door. (A good partner to have in the joint venture, which also includes the City of Burien, expected to open its new city hall/library at the four-block, mixed-use Burien Town Square this April, with more arts events planned.) Says Burien resident Johnson, “Seattle has its Olympic Sculpture Garden for its art superstars,” while this will be more DIY and inclusive. “There will be no ‘Don’t touch the art’ signs,” he adds. Fire performers, dancers, and music will attend the (snow-delayed) grand opening. After that, artists, new art, and volunteers are welcome. BRIAN MILLER

Since opening last year, the Olympic Sculpture Park has somehow eclipsed and subsumed the identity of Myrtle Edwards Park, which was established (with a different name) back in 1964, when SAM was still a small institution confined to Capitol Hill. The narrow old shoreline park was renamed in 1976 for the pioneering city councilwoman (1894–1969), and public art has been added at various junctures. Walk north of the OSP and you’ll find Michael Heizer’s Adjacent, Against, Upon(1976), which creates a grammar between three giant concrete slabs, obviously manmade, and three corresponding granite boulders (quarried from the Cascades and delivered by barge). The work is a series of prepositions running south to north, a delicate dance of heavyweights that tip the scales between 30 and 50 tons. Back in ’76, when the project was funded by the NEA, City Light, Virginia Wright, and the Seattle Arts Commission, it was “initially controversial,” according to the city Web site. Why controversial? I recall happily climbing on the rocks as a kid. But today I can imagine what might be called the Richard Serra Effect—it’s too big, too unfriendly, too invasive! It’s not a statue with a noble or smiling face (remember that patriotic bicentennial year). Three decades later, surrounded by well-tended gravel, the installation holds up remarkably well. Visitors picnic upon the rocks (or adjacent, or against); tourists pose with it; and unlike your snooty OSP, there’s no prohibition against touching or climbing on the things. Each smooth slab is a foundation. Each roughhewn boulder lies in a position of order or disorder, depending on which direction you walk past. The work either illustrates entropy or acts despite it. It was also reportedly the first public commission for Heizer (then 32), who for the past few decades has been remaking a big patch of Nevada desert into City, already considered one of America’s most significant examples of environmental art. (He’s continuing the tradition of his late friend and colleague Robert Smithson, famed for Spiral Jetty.) Adjacent, Against, Upon is a comparatively small-scale work in Heizer’s catalog; if it once seemed massive to Seattle pedestrians, it now reminds us how much larger the city has grown. BRIAN MILLER

It’s the day you’ve been waiting for. Your closest family and friends are gathered, sun-drenched in their finest, inhaling the sweet fragrance of the twin rows of rose bushes. The flower girl, her bow tied just so, swings her petal-filled basket. In the distance, the majestic Olympics hold vigil over the deep, sparkling waters of Elliott Bay, onto which a fireboat shoots a multi-streamed fountain salute. Yet on this, your wedding day, you feel a certain energy welling up within you. Sure, you’re all dressed up. But that’s nothing. To your left are the chin-up bars, the dip bars, the sit-up station, with its green enamel grating and shiny black foothold. And, of course, in the dirt: That rusted old iron dumbell, chained to the wooden pole, its two bulbous ends connected for eternity. A sweet foreboding. It calls you. And you answer. Just ten reps. Just the tip. This is why you chose the Rose Garden at Elliott Bay Park (at Pier 86 at the northern edge of Myrtle Edwards). DAMON AGNOS

Royal Purple Raceway benefits from incredible atmospheric conditions because of its proximity to Trinity Bay, which feeds the facility cool air. The track’s first NHRA national event, in fall 1988, established RPR as one of the sport’s quickest with NHRA’s first four-second Top Fuel quarter-mile pass and a new national record. Since then, the track has hosted a dizzying array of record runs, including the first sub-4.5-second Top Fuel quarter-mile pass by Larry Dixon in 1999. Pro Stock Motorcycles and Pro Mods will also compete at the event.
 
2010 recap: Matt Hagan’s first Funny Car win and Larry Dixon’s 50th in Top Fuel highlighted a spectacular race day. Jeg Coughlin Jr. and Andrew Hines earned respective wins in Pro Stock and Pro Stock Motorcycle. From the opening round of Top Fuel through the final rounds, the day was filled with intense action, wild races, and upsets aplenty.
 
How to Get There: Baytown is about 25 miles east of downtown Houston. From downtown Houston, take I-10 east to SH 99 Grand Parkway (Exit 799) and go south to FM 565 (approximately 2 miles). Take FM 565 west (right), and the track is on the right.
 
Visitor Information: Baytown Chamber of Commerce, 281-422-8359
